blocks.body:
Vector calculus ends with a collection of integral theorems that look alike but are stated separately: the fundamental theorem of calculus, Green's theorem in the plane, the Kelvin–Stokes theorem for surfaces and the divergence theorem for solids (see [[vector-calculus]]). Each says that integrating some kind of derivative over a region equals integrating the original object over the boundary of the region. Differential forms are the objects that make this a single statement.

The idea is to stop integrating functions and start integrating things that already know how to measure. A $1$-form eats a small arrow and returns a number, so it can be summed along a curve. A $2$-form eats two small arrows and returns a signed area, so it can be summed over a surface. One derivative $d$ acts on all of them, and one theorem, $\int_M d\omega=\int_{\partial M}\omega$, covers every case.

blocks.title: Things you integrate along curves
blocks.body:
In the plane, $dx$ is the function that takes a vector $v=(v_1,v_2)$ and returns its first component $v_1$; similarly $dy(v)=v_2$. A $1$-form is an expression $\omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy$ with smooth functions $P,Q$; at the point $p$ it sends $v$ to $P(p)v_1+Q(p)v_2$.

To integrate $\omega$ along a curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}^2$, chop the curve into tiny steps. On each step the curve moves by approximately the velocity $\gamma'(t)\,\Delta t$, and $\omega$ assigns that step the number $\omega_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t))\,\Delta t$. Adding up and refining gives
$$\int_\gamma \omega=\int_a^b \Big(P(\gamma(t))\,x'(t)+Q(\gamma(t))\,y'(t)\Big)\,dt,$$
which is exactly the line integral of the vector field $(P,Q)$. For example, with $\omega=-y\,dx+x\,dy$ and the unit circle $\gamma(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)$, $0\le t\le 2\pi$, the integrand is $\sin^2t+\cos^2t=1$ and $\int_\gamma\omega=2\pi$.

Two features are already visible. The answer does not depend on how fast we traverse the curve, only on its direction: reversing the direction flips the sign. And the integrand needed no lengths or angles, only the derivative of the parametrisation. These two features, orientation and independence from any metric, persist in every dimension.

blocks.title: Wedge products: signed areas and volumes
blocks.body:
To integrate over surfaces we need something that eats two vectors. Define
$$(dx\wedge dy)(v,w)=v_1w_2-v_2w_1=\det\begin{pmatrix}v_1&w_1\\ v_2&w_2\end{pmatrix},$$
the signed area of the parallelogram spanned by the projections of $v$ and $w$ to the $xy$-plane. Swapping $v$ and $w$ flips the sign, so $dy\wedge dx=-dx\wedge dy$, and in particular $dx\wedge dx=0$. In general, for $1$-forms $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k$ the product $\alpha_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\alpha_k$ sends $(v_1,\dots,v_k)$ to $\det[\alpha_i(v_j)]$. This is the exterior algebra of [[tensor-products]], applied to the dual of each tangent space.

In $\mathbb{R}^n$ write $dx_I=dx_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_{i_k}$ for an increasing multi-index $I=(i_1< \dots< i_k)$. Every alternating $k$-linear form on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a unique combination of these, so the space of such forms has dimension $\binom nk$. In $\mathbb{R}^3$ that gives dimensions $1,3,3,1$ for $k=0,1,2,3$: functions, objects like $P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz$, objects like $A\,dy\wedge dz+B\,dz\wedge dx+C\,dx\wedge dy$, and multiples of $dx\wedge dy\wedge dz$. That count, three and three, is why vector calculus can get away with using vector fields for both $1$-forms and $2$-forms.

The determinant hidden inside the wedge product is what makes the change-of-variables formula of [[multiple-integrals]] automatic. In polar coordinates $x=r\cos\theta$, $y=r\sin\theta$ we have $dx=\cos\theta\,dr-r\sin\theta\,d\theta$ and $dy=\sin\theta\,dr+r\cos\theta\,d\theta$. Multiplying out and using $dr\wedge dr=d\theta\wedge d\theta=0$,
$$dx\wedge dy=(r\cos^2\theta+r\sin^2\theta)\,dr\wedge d\theta=r\,dr\wedge d\theta.$$
The Jacobian factor $r$ appears without being asked for.

blocks.title: Differential form
blocks.body:
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be open. A differential $k$-form on $U$ is an expression
$$\omega=\sum_{I}f_I\,dx_I,$$
summed over increasing multi-indices $I$ of length $k$, with smooth functions $f_I:U\to\mathbb{R}$. At each point $p$ it is the alternating $k$-linear map $(v_1,\dots,v_k)\mapsto\sum_I f_I(p)\,dx_I(v_1,\dots,v_k)$. A $0$-form is a smooth function. The wedge product of forms is computed by multiplying out and using $dx_i\wedge dx_j=-dx_j\wedge dx_i$; for a $k$-form $\alpha$ and an $l$-form $\beta$ one gets $\beta\wedge\alpha=(-1)^{kl}\alpha\wedge\beta$.

Meaning: a $k$-form is a smoothly varying rule for measuring oriented $k$-dimensional volume, ready to be integrated over $k$-dimensional objects.

blocks.title: Exterior derivative
blocks.body:
For a function $f$, $df=\sum_{j=1}^n \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_j}\,dx_j$. For a $k$-form $\omega=\sum_I f_I\,dx_I$,
$$d\omega=\sum_I df_I\wedge dx_I=\sum_I\sum_{j=1}^n\frac{\partial f_I}{\partial x_j}\,dx_j\wedge dx_I .$$
It is linear and satisfies the Leibniz rule $d(\alpha\wedge\beta)=d\alpha\wedge\beta+(-1)^k\alpha\wedge d\beta$ for a $k$-form $\alpha$.

Meaning: $d\omega$ measures how $\omega$ fails to cancel around the boundary of a tiny $(k+1)$-dimensional box, which is exactly what the Stokes theorem turns into a global statement.

blocks.title: d squared is zero
blocks.body: For every smooth $k$-form $\omega$ on an open set of $\mathbb{R}^n$, $d(d\omega)=0$.

blocks.title: Proof that d∘d = 0
blocks.body:
By linearity it suffices to take $\omega=f\,dx_I$. Then $d\omega=\sum_j \partial_j f\,dx_j\wedge dx_I$, and since $d(dx_I)=0$ (its coefficient is the constant $1$),
$$d(d\omega)=\sum_{i,j}\partial_i\partial_j f\;dx_i\wedge dx_j\wedge dx_I .$$
The terms with $i=j$ vanish because $dx_i\wedge dx_i=0$. The terms with $i\ne j$ come in pairs $(i,j)$ and $(j,i)$; their coefficients $\partial_i\partial_jf$ and $\partial_j\partial_if$ are equal by the symmetry of mixed partial derivatives for smooth functions (see [[partial-derivatives]]), while $dx_j\wedge dx_i=-dx_i\wedge dx_j$. So each pair cancels and $d(d\omega)=0$.

blocks.title: The dictionary with vector calculus
blocks.body:
In $\mathbb{R}^3$ match $1$-forms with vector fields by $F=(F_1,F_2,F_3)\leftrightarrow F_1\,dx+F_2\,dy+F_3\,dz$, and $2$-forms with vector fields by $G\leftrightarrow G_1\,dy\wedge dz+G_2\,dz\wedge dx+G_3\,dx\wedge dy$. Direct computation from the definition gives:

1. For a function $f$, $df$ corresponds to $\nabla f$.
2. For a $1$-form, $d(F_1\,dx+F_2\,dy+F_3\,dz)$ corresponds to $\operatorname{curl}F$. For instance the $dy\wedge dz$ coefficient is $\partial_yF_3-\partial_zF_2$.
3. For a $2$-form, $$d(G_1\,dy\wedge dz+G_2\,dz\wedge dx+G_3\,dx\wedge dy)=(\partial_xG_1+\partial_yG_2+\partial_zG_3)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz$$, the divergence.

Under this dictionary $d\circ d=0$ becomes the two identities $\operatorname{curl}(\nabla f)=0$ and $\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{curl}F)=0$. In the plane, $d(P\,dx+Q\,dy)=(\partial_xQ-\partial_yP)\,dx\wedge dy$, the integrand of Green's theorem.

A form with $d\omega=0$ is called closed; a form with $\omega=d\eta$ for some $\eta$ is called exact. By $d\circ d=0$, exact forms are closed. Whether closed forms are exact depends on the shape of the domain, as the example "Closed but not exact" shows.

blocks.title: Pullback, orientation and integration
blocks.body:
If $\varphi:V\to U$ is smooth, with $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m$, the pullback $\varphi^*\omega$ is the form on $V$ obtained by substituting $x=\varphi(u)$: replace each coefficient $f(x)$ by $f(\varphi(u))$ and each $dx_i$ by $d\varphi_i=\sum_j \partial_{u_j}\varphi_i\,du_j$. The polar computation above was the pullback of $dx\wedge dy$. Pullback respects wedge products and commutes with the derivative: $d(\varphi^*\omega)=\varphi^*(d\omega)$.

Integration is defined by pulling back to a box. On a box $B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^k$ with its standard orientation, $\int_B f\,du_1\wedge\cdots\wedge du_k=\int_B f\,du_1\cdots du_k$, an ordinary multiple integral. For a parametrised $k$-dimensional piece $\varphi:B\to\mathbb{R}^n$, define $\int_\varphi\omega=\int_B\varphi^*\omega$. If $\psi$ is an orientation-preserving reparametrisation (positive Jacobian determinant), the change-of-variables formula shows that the answer is unchanged; if the Jacobian determinant is negative the sign flips. So a $k$-form can be integrated over any oriented $k$-dimensional manifold, by cutting it into parametrised pieces, or more cleanly with a partition of unity, as on [[smooth-manifolds]].

The boundary $\partial M$ of an oriented manifold with boundary gets the induced orientation: a basis $(v_1,\dots,v_{k-1})$ of the tangent space of $\partial M$ is positive if (outward normal, $v_1,\dots,v_{k-1}$) is positive for $M$. For a region in the plane this means the boundary is traversed with the region on the left.

blocks.title: The general Stokes theorem
blocks.body:
Let $M$ be an oriented smooth $k$-dimensional manifold with boundary, with $\partial M$ carrying the induced orientation, and let $\omega$ be a smooth $(k-1)$-form on $M$ with compact support. Then
$$\int_M d\omega=\int_{\partial M}\omega .$$
If $\partial M=\varnothing$ the right side is $0$. The same identity holds for a smooth singular $k$-chain $c$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$: $\int_c d\omega=\int_{\partial c}\omega$.

blocks.title: Proof for a cube, and how the general case follows
blocks.body:
Let $I^k=[0,1]^k$ with its standard orientation. For $j=1,\dots,k$ and $\alpha\in\{0,1\}$ let the face map $\iota_{j,\alpha}:I^{k-1}\to I^k$ insert $\alpha$ as the $j$-th coordinate, and define the oriented boundary $\partial I^k=\sum_{j,\alpha}(-1)^{j+\alpha}\iota_{j,\alpha}$. (For $k=2$ this is the square traversed counterclockwise.)

By linearity we may take $\omega=f\,dx_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\widehat{dx_i}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_k$, where the hat means that $dx_i$ is omitted. In $d\omega$ only $\partial_if\,dx_i$ survives the wedge with the remaining $dx$'s, and moving $dx_i$ into position $i$ past $i-1$ factors gives
$$d\omega=(-1)^{i-1}\,\partial_if\;dx_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_k .$$
Integrate first in $x_i$ using the one-variable fundamental theorem of calculus:
$$\int_{I^k}d\omega=(-1)^{i-1}\int_{I^{k-1}}\Big(f|_{x_i=1}-f|_{x_i=0}\Big)\,dx_1\cdots\widehat{dx_i}\cdots dx_k .$$
Now the boundary. On a face with $j\ne i$ the coordinate $x_j$ is constant, so $\iota_{j,\alpha}^*dx_j=0$; since $dx_j$ occurs in $\omega$, the pullback vanishes. On the faces $j=i$ the pullback is $f|_{x_i=\alpha}\,dt_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dt_{k-1}$. Hence
$$\int_{\partial I^k}\omega=(-1)^{i+1}\int f|_{x_i=1}+(-1)^{i}\int f|_{x_i=0},$$
which is the same expression. So the theorem holds for the cube.

For a singular cube, a smooth map $c=\varphi:I^k\to\mathbb{R}^n$ with $\partial c=\sum_{j,\alpha}(-1)^{j+\alpha}\varphi\circ\iota_{j,\alpha}$, the result follows by pulling back, since $$\int_c d\omega=\int_{I^k}\varphi^*d\omega=\int_{I^k}d(\varphi^*\omega)=\int_{\partial I^k}\varphi^*\omega=\int_{\partial c}\omega$$, and for chains by adding. For a manifold one writes $\omega$ as a finite sum of forms supported in coordinate charts using a partition of unity, applies the cube case (or a half-cube case at the boundary) in each chart, and adds; this last step is standard bookkeeping and is done carefully in Lee, chapter 16.

blocks.title: Green's theorem as a special case
blocks.body: Let $D$ be the closed unit disc and $\omega=-y\,dx+x\,dy$. Compute $\int_D d\omega$ and $\int_{\partial D}\omega$ separately and check that they agree. What does this say about area?
blocks.solution:
First, $d\omega=d(-y)\wedge dx+dx\wedge dy=-dy\wedge dx+dx\wedge dy=2\,dx\wedge dy$. So $\int_Dd\omega=2\cdot\operatorname{area}(D)=2\pi$.

The boundary circle with the induced orientation is traversed counterclockwise, $\gamma(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)$. Pulling back, $\gamma^*\omega=(-\sin t)(-\sin t\,dt)+\cos t(\cos t\,dt)=dt$, so $\int_{\partial D}\omega=\int_0^{2\pi}dt=2\pi$. The two sides agree.

The same computation for any region $R$ with piecewise smooth boundary gives the area formula $\operatorname{area}(R)=\tfrac12\oint_{\partial R}(x\,dy-y\,dx)$. This is the principle behind the planimeter, a mechanical instrument that measures area by tracing the boundary.

blocks.title: Flux through the sphere
blocks.body: Let $\omega=x\,dy\wedge dz+y\,dz\wedge dx+z\,dx\wedge dy$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$ and let $S$ be the unit sphere, oriented as the boundary of the unit ball $B$. Compute $\int_S\omega$ directly with the parametrisation $\varphi(\theta,\phi)=(\sin\theta\cos\phi,\ \sin\theta\sin\phi,\ \cos\theta)$, $0\le\theta\le\pi$, $0\le\phi\le2\pi$, and compare with $\int_Bd\omega$.
blocks.solution:
Pulling back a $2$-form $A\,dy\wedge dz+B\,dz\wedge dx+C\,dx\wedge dy$ along $\varphi$ gives $(A,B,C)\cdot(\varphi_\theta\times\varphi_\phi)\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$, because each $dx_i\wedge dx_j$ pulls back to a $2\times2$ minor of the Jacobian. Here
$$\varphi_\theta\times\varphi_\phi=\sin\theta\,(\sin\theta\cos\phi,\ \sin\theta\sin\phi,\ \cos\theta)=\sin\theta\,\varphi,$$
which points outward, so the order $(\theta,\phi)$ matches the induced orientation. With $(A,B,C)=\varphi$ the pullback is $\sin\theta\,|\varphi|^2\,d\theta\wedge d\phi=\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$, and
$$\int_S\omega=\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^\pi\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi=4\pi .$$
On the other side, $d\omega=(1+1+1)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz$, so $\int_Bd\omega=3\cdot\tfrac43\pi=4\pi$. This is the divergence theorem for the field $(x,y,z)$, whose divergence is $3$.

blocks.title: Closed but not exact
blocks.body:
On the punctured plane $U=\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{0\}$ let
$$\omega=\frac{-y\,dx+x\,dy}{x^2+y^2}.$$
Show that $d\omega=0$ but that $\omega\ne df$ for every smooth function $f$ on $U$. Then show that on the slit plane, $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the closed negative $x$-axis removed, $\omega$ is exact.
blocks.solution:
Write $\omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy$ with $P=-y/(x^2+y^2)$ and $Q=x/(x^2+y^2)$. Then
$$\partial_xQ=\frac{y^2-x^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2}=\partial_yP,$$
so $d\omega=(\partial_xQ-\partial_yP)\,dx\wedge dy=0$.

Suppose $\omega=df$ on $U$. For the unit circle $\gamma$, a closed curve, $\int_\gamma df=\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{d}{dt}f(\gamma(t))\,dt=f(\gamma(2\pi))-f(\gamma(0))=0$. (This is Stokes for a $1$-dimensional manifold with empty boundary.) But $\gamma^*\omega=dt$ exactly as in the Green's theorem example, because $x^2+y^2=1$ on the circle, so $\int_\gamma\omega=2\pi\ne0$. Contradiction.

On the slit plane every point can be written uniquely as $(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)$ with $-\pi< \theta< \pi$, and $\theta$ is a smooth function there. Differentiating $\tan\theta=y/x$ (or using the polar pullback) gives $d\theta=\omega$. So $\omega$ is exact on the slit plane, and $\int_\gamma\omega=2\pi$ is the total change in angle around the hole. The failure of exactness on $U$ detects the hole; making this precise is the start of de Rham cohomology.

blocks.body:
- Order matters: $dx\wedge dy=-dy\wedge dx$. Reordering a wedge product without tracking signs is the most common source of errors, especially in the induced boundary orientation.
- A $k$-form can only be integrated over a $k$-dimensional oriented object. Integrating $dx\wedge dy$ "along a curve" has no meaning, and without an orientation even $\int_M\omega$ is only defined up to sign.
- Closed does not imply exact. The implication holds on open sets that are star-shaped (Poincaré lemma) but fails on the punctured plane, as shown in the example "Closed but not exact".
- The theorem needs compact support or a compact manifold. Take $M=(0,1)$, which has no boundary points in the manifold sense, and the $0$-form $\omega=x$, which does not have compact support in $M$: then $\int_M d\omega=\int_0^1 dx=1$, not $0$, because the boundary points have been thrown away.
- $d$ of a $1$-form is not a gradient. Under the dictionary it is a curl, and the dictionary between $2$-forms and vector fields uses the Euclidean metric and orientation of $\mathbb{R}^3$, while $d$ itself needs neither.

Forms are the natural integrands on [[smooth-manifolds]], where they are defined chart by chart and the coordinate formula for $d$ turns out not to depend on the chart. On a Riemannian manifold ([[riemannian-geometry]]) the metric adds a volume form and the Hodge star, which converts $k$-forms into $(n-k)$-forms and recovers gradient, curl and divergence on any manifold. The quotient of closed $k$-forms by exact ones is the de Rham cohomology; de Rham's theorem says it agrees with real singular cohomology, linking calculus to [[homology]]. The Gauss–Bonnet theorem ([[gauss-bonnet]]) can be proved by applying Stokes to a connection $1$-form whose derivative is curvature times area. In physics, the electromagnetic field is a $2$-form $F$ on spacetime, and two of Maxwell's equations are simply $dF=0$; the other two say $d{\star}F$ is the current $3$-form, up to constants and sign conventions. In complex analysis, $d(f\,dz)=\partial_{\bar z}f\,d\bar z\wedge dz$, which vanishes for holomorphic $f$; this gives Cauchy's theorem (see [[holomorphic]]).

1. Compute $d\omega$ for $\omega=xy\,dz+yz\,dx+zx\,dy$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$, and check that $d(d\omega)=0$.
2. Show that the pullback of $dx\wedge dy\wedge dz$ under spherical coordinates $$(\rho,\theta,\phi)\mapsto(\rho\sin\theta\cos\phi,\rho\sin\theta\sin\phi,\rho\cos\theta)$$ is $\rho^2\sin\theta\,d\rho\wedge d\theta\wedge d\phi$.
3. Use the Stokes theorem to show that the integral of an exact $2$-form $d\eta$ over the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is $0$, and deduce that the form $\omega/(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{3/2}$, with $\omega$ as in the sphere example, is closed but not exact on $\mathbb{R}^3\setminus\{0\}$.
4. Write down $\partial I^2$ explicitly as four oriented edges and check that it is the boundary of the unit square traversed counterclockwise.
